title: Prefix trees
objectives: Build a trie and use it for prefix search and word lookups.

screens.title: Shared beginnings
screens.prose: Four words, `tea`, `ten`, `to` and `inn`, are stored letter by letter. Words that begin alike share their first letters. A node marked *word* is where a word ends.
screens.question: How many nodes are there, not counting the root?

widget.accept: 8: t, te, tea, ten, to, i, in and inn.
widget.label: Nodes

hints.text: Count the pills below the root.
`tea` and `ten` share the nodes t and te.
t, te, tea, ten, to on one side and i, in, inn on the other: 8.

feedback.correct: Eight nodes: one per distinct prefix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each node once, however many words pass through it.

byKey.letters: You counted every letter of every word: 3 + 3 + 2 + 3. Shared beginnings such as t and te are stored once.
byKey.words: You counted words. Each word needs a node per letter, though shared letters are stored once.
byKey.root: You counted the root as well. Leave it out: it holds no letter.

explain.text: Each node stands for one prefix: t, te, tea, ten, to, i, in, inn. `tea` and `ten` share t and te, and `to` shares t. So there are 8 nodes, against 11 letters in the four words.

screens.title: Insert one at a time
screens.prose: Slide through the inserts and watch which nodes each word adds. Greyed nodes do not exist yet.
screens.question: Tap the nodes that exist after inserting only `tea` and `ten`.

hints.text: Move the slider to the second word and look at what is not grey.

feedback.correct: `ten` reused t and te and added only n.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the nodes that `tea` makes, then what `ten` adds.

byKey.t-o: `to` has not been inserted yet, so its o does not exist.
byKey.i: `inn` comes last. Its nodes do not exist after two inserts.
byKey.t-e-n: `ten` adds its n under te. Include it.
byKey.t: Every word starting with t passes through this node. Include it.

explain.text: `tea` made t, te and tea. `ten` walked t and te, found them, and created only its n. Inserting creates a node only where the walk finds nothing.

screens.title: Ends matter
screens.prose: `search(word)` walks the letters and then checks the *word* mark. `starts_with(prefix)` walks the letters and checks only that it arrived. The four words are inserted.
screens.question: What do `search('te')` and `starts_with('te')` return?

options.why: You found the node te and stopped. `search` also checks that a word ends there, and none does.
`starts_with` only asks that the walk arrives. The node te exists.
These are swapped. The walk reaches te, but no word ends there.

hints.text: Is there a node for te?
The node te has no *word* mark.
The walk arrives, so `starts_with` is `True`. No word ends at te, so `search` is `False`.

feedback.correct: te is a prefix of two words but not a word itself.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate arriving at a node from a word ending there.

byKey.b: You treated arriving as finding a word. Only tea, ten, to and inn carry the *word* mark.

explain.text: Both calls walk t then e and arrive. `starts_with` stops there and says `True`. `search` also reads the end mark, which te does not have, so it says `False`.

screens.title: How big can it get
screens.prose: A trie stores 1,000 words, each 10 letters long. Each insert adds at most one node per letter. Shared prefixes only make it smaller.

state.caption: Each word adds at most one node per letter

screens.question: What is the most nodes the trie can need, not counting the root?

widget.accept: 10,000: 1,000 words times at most 10 new nodes each.
widget.label: Nodes at most

hints.text: How many nodes can one 10-letter word add?
With no shared prefix, every letter needs a new node, as tea needed three.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the words by the most nodes each can add.

byKey.alpha: 26 is the most children one node can have. The question asks for all the nodes.
byKey.words: You gave one node per word. A word needs a node per letter.
byKey.alpha2: That is 26 letters times 10 levels. Different words can use the same letter at the same depth in different branches.

explain.text: Each insert walks 10 letters and creates at most 10 nodes, so 10,000 is the ceiling. A search then costs 10 steps, whatever the number of words. A plain list would compare the word against up to 1,000 others.

screens.title: Write the trie
screens.prose: Write a `Trie` with `insert`, `search`, `starts_with` and `count_prefix`. `count_prefix` returns how many distinct inserted words start with the prefix. Inserting a word twice counts once. The empty prefix counts every word, and `starts_with('')` is `True` even for an empty trie.

state.caption: A node is a dict: a letter maps to a child

screens.question: Write the `Trie` class. Each node can be a dict from a letter to its child.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests through `run_trie(ops)`. It builds one `Trie`, replays the operations and lists every result but those of `insert`. They cover an empty trie, a repeated insert and the empty prefix.

hints.text: What does each node need besides its children?
A flag for a word ending here, and a count of words passing through.
Store children as `node[ch]`, the end flag as `node['#end']` and the count as `node['#n']`. Add to the counts only when the word was not already marked.

feedback.correct: Each operation walks one node per letter: $O(L)$ for a word of length $L$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 inserts three words and asks about te. Make `insert` build the nodes first.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 searches app after only apple. The walk arrives, but no word ends there yet.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 inserts inn twice. Count only when the end mark was not already set.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 uses the empty prefix. The walk then stays at the root, which counts every word.

explain.text: `insert` walks and creates, then marks the end and bumps the counts only for a new word. `search`, `starts_with` and `count_prefix` share one walk that returns the node or `None`. Every call costs one step per letter.

screens.title: Counting prefixes
screens.prose: Each node keeps a count of the words that pass through it. `count_prefix` walks to the prefix and reads that count. Now `inn` is inserted a second time.
screens.question: What should `count_prefix('in')` return now?

options.why: You added to the counts on the second insert too. `inn` was already a word, so nothing changes.
You counted the nodes i, in and inn. The count is of words, not nodes.
in is not a word, but `inn` passes through it, so the count is not 0.

hints.text: Is `inn` a new word the second time?
The end mark on inn is already set.
A repeat insert finds the mark set and changes no count, so the answer stays 1.

feedback.correct: One distinct word starts with in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count distinct words that start with in.

byKey.b: You counted the repeat. Check the end mark first, and add to the counts only for a new word.

explain.text: The second insert walks i, in, inn and finds the end mark already set. So it skips the counting step. `count_prefix('in')` reads 1.

screens.title: A prefix is not a word
screens.prose: Only `apple` has been inserted. A learner's `search` walks the letters and returns `True` if the walk arrives.
screens.question: What should `search('app')` return?

options.why: You walked a, p, p and found a node. No word ends there: only apple was inserted.
Every letter of app exists in the trie, so the walk never reads a missing child.

options.text: It depends on the order of inserts
options.why: Only one word was inserted. The end marks, not the order, decide.

hints.text: Which node carries the *word* mark?
Only the last e of apple is marked.
The walk reaches the second p, but that node has no end mark. So `search` is `False`.

feedback.correct: app is a prefix of apple, not a word in the trie.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the end mark on the node you reach.

byKey.b: You returned `True` because the walk arrived. That answers `starts_with('app')`, not `search('app')`.

explain.text: The walk a, p, p arrives at a node with no end mark, so `search` must return `False`. The learner's version answers `starts_with` instead. After `insert('app')` the same node is marked and `search('app')` turns `True`.

canvas.caption: Arrived, but no word ends here

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
What you wrote, as a pattern:

```python
node = root
for ch in word:
    node = node.setdefault(ch, {})   # create
node['#end'] = True
# search: walk, then check '#end'
# prefix: walk, and only check arrival
```
screens.question: Put the steps of `insert` with prefix counts in order. Leave out the step that does not belong.

lines.text: For each letter, step to its child, creating it if missing
If the last node is not already a word end, mark it
Only then add one to the count of every node on the path
Add one to each node's count as you walk, before checking the mark
lines.why: A repeated insert would then count twice. Check the end mark first, and count only a new word.

feedback.correct: Walk, create, mark, and count only a new word.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The counting depends on whether the word is new.

byKey.d1: You counted during the walk. That counts `inn` twice when it is inserted twice.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs. Only counting during the walk is wrong.

explain.text: The walk creates what is missing, so inserting costs one step per letter. The end mark separates words from prefixes. Counting after the mark check keeps repeats out of `count_prefix`.

screens.title: Suggest symbols
screens.prose: An order-entry box suggests what a trader may mean as they type. It shows the first `k` matches in alphabetical order. The tests use short words in place of symbols. Repeats in the list count once.

state.caption: Below te, in alphabetical order: tea, team, tear, ten

screens.question: Write `top_completions(words, prefix, k)`. Return the `k` alphabetically smallest distinct words starting with `prefix`, or fewer. Return `[]` for no match or `k = 0`.

widget.starter:
def top_completions(words, prefix, k):
    return [w for w in words if w.startswith(prefix)][:k]
widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests: repeats, `k` larger than the matches, the empty prefix and no match. Others have `k = 0`, an empty list, and a prefix that is a word.

hints.text: After walking to the prefix, in what order should you visit the children?
Visit the children in sorted letter order, and record a word before its children.
Depth-first from the prefix node: if the node ends a word, append it; then recurse into `sorted` children. Stop once you hold `k`.

feedback.correct: Walk to the prefix, then a sorted depth-first search that stops at `k`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 has tea twice and the words out of order. Use a set, then visit children alphabetically.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 asks for ab, which is a word and a prefix. Record a node's own word before its children.

explain.text: A word comes before every longer word that starts with it, so we record a node before its children. Visiting children in sorted order then yields alphabetical order. The search stops after `k` words, so a short list costs little.

screens.title: When a sorted list wins
screens.prose: A desk has 4,000 symbols, changed once a day. It only asks prefix queries, and memory is tight. In Python a trie node is a dict, which costs far more memory than a short string.
screens.question: Which structure fits best?

options.text: A trie, because it is always faster
options.why: For 4,000 symbols both are fast: `bisect` makes about 12 comparisons and a trie walk one step per letter. The trie's dicts cost far more memory.
A set answers whole-word lookups. It cannot list the symbols that start with a prefix.
That reads all 4,000 symbols on every keystroke. A sorted list needs about 12 comparisons.

hints.text: What does a sorted list already give you for a prefix?
All the words with one prefix sit next to each other in a sorted list.
`bisect_left` finds where the prefix would go; the matches follow it. That is $O(\log n)$ with no extra memory.

feedback.correct: A sorted list is small, and `bisect` makes about $\log_2 4000 \approx 12$ comparisons.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weigh memory as well as speed.

byKey.b: You chose speed alone. At this size the speeds are close, and the trie costs more memory.

explain.text: In a sorted list, words sharing a prefix sit side by side. `bisect_left` finds the first one in about 12 comparisons. A trie pays off with frequent inserts or removals, which cost one step per letter instead of shifting a list, and with queries that branch, such as a `?` in a pattern.

ideas: A trie stores words letter by letter; words that begin alike share nodes. Each node is a dict from a letter to a child.
`search` walks and checks the end mark; `starts_with` walks and checks only that it arrived.
A count on each node, raised once per new word, answers `count_prefix` in one walk.

formula.name: Cost of an operation
formula.tex: O(L) \text{ for a word or prefix of length } L
formula.note: Independent of how many words are stored. Memory is at most one node per letter inserted.

summary.trap: Returning `True` because the walk arrived answers `starts_with` instead: `app` is not a word just because `apple` is.

byKey.words: You counted words. A word needs a node per letter.

The walk s, e, l arrives, so `starts_with` is `True`.

quiz.prose: We insert `bid`, `bid` and `bids`, with counts kept as in the lesson.
quiz.question: What does `count_prefix('bid')` return?

widget.accept: 2: bid and bids; the repeat counts once.
widget.label: Count

feedback.correct: Two distinct words start with bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count distinct inserted words.

byKey.repeat: You counted the second bid. It found the end mark set, so it changed no count.

explain.text: The first bid and then bids each add one to the node bid. The repeat finds bid already marked and adds nothing. So the count is 2.

quiz.prose: 4,000 symbols are kept in a sorted list. `bisect_left` finds where a prefix would go by halving the range each step.
quiz.question: About how many comparisons does one `bisect_left` make?

options.why: That is the average cost of a scan. `bisect` halves the range at every step.
That is a scan of every symbol.
That is $\sqrt{4000}$. Halving gives a logarithm, not a square root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count how many halvings take 4,000 down to 1.

explain.text: Each comparison halves the range, so it takes $\log_2 4000 \approx 12$ steps. $2^{12} = 4096$ is just above 4,000. A trie walk for a three-letter prefix takes 3 steps, but costs more memory.
